_note: AI-drafted Yoruba A1 grammar lessons for Langi, not yet reviewed by a native speaker. Slugs match the yo catalog in lib/grammar.ts. Drill cues give the meaning, never the answer. Seeded by `npx tsx scripts/seed-grammar-ng.ts yo`. In examples, `fr` holds the Yoruba sentence (field name kept from the original schema).

lessons.summary: Mo, o, ó, a, ẹ and wọ́n stand before the verb as I, you, he/she/it, we, you (plural) and they.
lessons.explanation:
Yoruba verbs never change their ending. The subject pronoun before the verb does the work. The short forms are: mo (I), o (you, one person), ó (he, she, it), a (we), ẹ (you, more than one person or a respected elder) and wọ́n (they).

Ó means he, she or it. Yoruba does not mark gender in pronouns, so only the context tells you which one is meant.

Tones matter. Compare o (you, mid tone) with ó (he/she, high tone): O dára means you are fine, Ó dára means he/she/it is fine. Always write the tone marks when you can.

The long forms (èmi, ìwọ, òun, àwa, ẹ̀yin, àwọn) are used for emphasis or on their own, for example Èmi ni (It is me). In normal sentences use the short forms.

examples.en: Thank you (to more than one person or an elder).

drills.prompt: ___ lọ sí ọjà. (I went to the market)
___ ń kọ́ Yorùbá. (We are learning Yoruba)

lessons.summary: Tense words go before the verb: ń (is doing), ti (has done), máa or yóò (will do).
lessons.explanation:
The verb itself stays the same. A small word before it tells you when and how the action happens.

ń shows an action in progress: Mo ń jẹun (I am eating). ti shows it is already done: Mo ti jẹun (I have eaten). máa shows the future: Mo máa lọ (I will go). Yóò also marks the future and is common in more formal speech: Yóò rọ̀ lọ́la (It will rain tomorrow).

For a habit, combine them: máa ń. Mo máa ń jẹ ìrẹsì means I usually eat rice.

With no marker, a plain action verb usually points to the past: Mo lọ means I went. Time words such as lánàá (yesterday) and lọ́la (tomorrow) make it clear.

drills.prompt: Mo ___ lọ lọ́la. (I will go tomorrow)
Wọ́n ___ kọ lẹ́tà. (They are writing a letter)

lessons.summary: Put ò or kò before the verb to say not: Mi ò lọ (I don't go), Kò wá (He/she did not come).
lessons.explanation:
To make a sentence negative, a negative word goes before the verb, and it takes the place of the pronoun in several persons.

The forms are: mi ò (I do not), o ò (you do not), kò (he/she/it does not), a ò (we do not), ẹ ò (you, plural, do not) and wọn ò (they do not).

Mi ò mọ̀ means I do not know. Kò wá means he/she did not come. Wọn ò jẹun means they did not eat or they do not eat.

The same negative form covers the past and the present. Use a time word or the context to show which one you mean.

examples.fr: A ò lọ sí ilé ìwé.
examples.en: We are not going to school.

lessons.summary: Use jẹ́ for what someone is, wà for where someone is, and ni to point out who or what it is.
lessons.explanation:
English uses one verb, to be. Yoruba splits it into three.

jẹ́ links a person to an identity or job: Mo jẹ́ dókítà (I am a doctor). wà says where something is, or that it exists: Ó wà nílé (He/she is at home). ni points something out: Èyí ni ilé mi (This is my house), Òun ni olùkọ́ mi (That is my teacher).

Before an adjective you need no verb at all: Ilé náà ńlá means The house is big.

drills.prompt: Wọ́n ___ ní Èkó. (They are in Lagos)
Èyí ___ ilé mi. (This is my house)

lessons.summary: Ṣé opens a yes/no question. Kí, ta, ibo and mélòó ask what, who, where and how many.
lessons.explanation:
For a yes/no question, put ṣé at the front: Ṣé o ti jẹun? (Have you eaten?). You can also use a rising tone with no extra word.

Question words usually come first or sit before ni: Kí ni orúkọ rẹ? (What is your name?), Ta ni ó wá? (Who came?), Ibo ni o ń gbé? (Where do you live?), Mélòó ni èyí? (How much is this?).

The words you will use most: kí (what), ta (who), ibo (where), nígbà wo (when), kí nìdí (why), mélòó (how many, how much).

drills.prompt: ___ ni orúkọ rẹ? (What is your name?)
___ ni o ń gbé? (Where do you live?)

lessons.summary: Yoruba nouns do not change for plural. Use àwọn, a number, kan (a) or náà (the).
lessons.explanation:
A Yoruba noun looks the same in the singular and the plural: ọmọ means child or children.

To make the plural clear, put àwọn before the noun: àwọn ọmọ (the children). With a number you need nothing else: ìwé mẹ́ta (three books).

There is no a or the in front of the noun. After it, kan means a or one: ọmọ kan (a child). náà means the, as in ilé náà (the house).

lessons.summary: Put the owner after the thing: ilé bàbá mi (my father's house), ìwé rẹ (your book).
lessons.explanation:
Yoruba has no apostrophe-s. Write the thing first and the owner after it: ilé bàbá mi (father's house, my father's house).

For my, your and so on, put these words after the noun: mi (my), rẹ (your, one person), rẹ̀ (his, her), wa (our), yín (your, plural) and wọn (their). Watch the tone: ìwé rẹ is your book, and ìwé rẹ̀ is his or her book.

lessons.summary: Adjectives come after the noun: ilé ńlá (a big house), aṣọ pupa (red cloth).
lessons.explanation:
In Yoruba the adjective follows the noun: ilé ńlá (house big, a big house), ọmọ kékeré (a small child), aṣọ pupa (red cloth), ọkọ̀ tuntun (a new car).

The adjective does not change for number. If you want the, add náà at the very end: ilé ńlá náà means the big house.
